title: Retrieval-augmented generation
summary: RAG adds a non-parametric memory (a searchable index of text) to a model whose own knowledge is frozen in its weights. A bi-encoder embeds chunks once, so retrieval is a nearest-neighbour search by cosine similarity, made fast by approximate indexes such as HNSW; a cross-encoder can rerank the top few. Retrieved chunks are just tokens in the context that attention reads, so retrieval quality, and even position, decide what the model can use.
llm_link: Your RAG apps are this pipeline. When a RAG answer is wrong, check recall@k first: if the right chunk was not retrieved the model never saw it, and if a wrong chunk was retrieved the model reads it as faithfully as a right one.
key_ideas: Parametric memory (weights): fixed at training, hard to update or cite. Non-parametric memory (an index of documents): updated by editing text. Lewis et al. (2020) combined both.

Bi-encoder retrieval: query and chunks are embedded separately, so chunk vectors are precomputed. With unit-length vectors, cosine similarity is a dot product, and top-k is a matrix-vector product plus a sort.
Approximate nearest neighbour (e.g. HNSW, layered neighbour graphs searched greedily) trades a small recall loss for large speed-ups.
Cross-encoders read query and chunk together: more accurate, too slow for the whole corpus, so they rerank a shortlist. Hybrid search adds keyword scores (BM25) for exact names and codes.

Inside the model, retrieved text is ordinary context that attention reads. Liu et al. (Lost in the Middle) found models often use information at the start or end of a long context better than in the middle.
Evaluate in two parts: retrieval (recall@k) and generation (faithfulness to the retrieved text).

quiz.q: Predict the result: unit vectors q = [0.6, 0.8] and c = [0.8, 0.6]. What is their cosine similarity?
quiz.explain: For unit vectors cosine similarity is the dot product: 0.6·0.8 + 0.8·0.6 = 0.96.

quiz.q: Why can a bi-encoder's chunk embeddings be computed once and stored, while a cross-encoder's scores cannot?
options: The bi-encoder encodes each chunk without seeing the query; a cross-encoder must read query and chunk together
quiz.explain: Because the chunk side never depends on the query, its vector is reusable. A cross-encoder's score depends on the pair, so it has to be recomputed for every query.

quiz.q: Your RAG system answers wrongly. Retrieval logs show the correct passage was ranked 40th and you pass the top 5 to the model. What should you fix first?
options: Retrieval: recall@5 failed, so the model never saw the answer
quiz.explain: The model cannot use a passage that is not in its context. Improve retrieval (better embeddings, hybrid search, reranking, more candidates) before touching generation.

quiz.q: What did the Lost in the Middle study observe?
options: Models often used relevant information best at the start or end of a long context and worse in the middle
Only the last token of the context matters
quiz.explain: Performance often followed a U shape over the position of the relevant passage, which is one reason rerankers put the best chunks first.

quiz.q: In the transformer, what happens to retrieved chunks pasted into the prompt?
options: They become ordinary tokens in the context that attention can read when generating
They are stored in a separate memory module
They are converted to a single vector
quiz.explain: Nothing special: they are tokens, with keys and values in the KV cache like any other text, and attention draws on them.

problems.title: Cosine top-k (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Write top_k(query, chunks, k). query has shape (d,) and chunks has shape (n, d), one row per chunk. Return the indices of the k chunks with the highest cosine similarity, best first.

Plan: scale every row of chunks and the query to unit length, then one matrix-vector product gives all the cosine similarities at once.

chunks = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
top_k(np.array([1.0, 0.2]), chunks, 2)   # [0, 2]

tests.name: example
tests.code:
import numpy as np
chunks = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
out = top_k(np.array([1.0, 0.2]), chunks, 2)
assert out is not None, 'top_k returned None'
assert list(out) == [0, 2], f'expected [0, 2], got {list(out)}. Check the order: best (largest similarity) first.'

tests.name: length does not matter, direction does
tests.code:
import numpy as np
chunks = np.array([[10.0, 0.0], [0.6, 0.8]])
out = top_k(np.array([0.6, 0.8]), chunks, 1)
assert list(out) == [1], f'chunk 0 is long but points elsewhere; cosine similarity ignores length. Expected [1], got {list(out)}. Did you normalise the rows?'

tests.name: returns exactly k
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); C = rng.normal(size=(50, 8)); q = rng.normal(size=8)
out = top_k(q, C, 5)
assert len(out) == 5, f'expected 5 indices, got {len(out)}'

tests.name: matches brute force
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1); C = rng.normal(size=(30, 6)); q = rng.normal(size=6)
sims = [c @ q / (np.linalg.norm(c) * np.linalg.norm(q)) for c in C]
exp = sorted(range(30), key=lambda i: -sims[i])[:4]
assert list(out := top_k(q, C, 4)) == exp, f'expected {exp}, got {list(out)}'

hints: C = chunks / np.linalg.norm(chunks, axis=1, keepdims=True); keepdims keeps the shape (n, 1) so the division broadcasts over each row.
np.argsort(sims) sorts ascending. Reverse it with [::-1], then take [:k].
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def top_k(query, chunks, k):
    C = chunks / np.linalg.norm(chunks, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    q = query / np.linalg.norm(query)
    sims = C @ q
    return np.argsort(sims)[::-1][:k]

problems.title: Recall at k
problems.prompt:
For each test question you have the retriever's ranked list of chunk ids and the set of ids that actually contain the answer. Write recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k): the fraction of questions for which at least one relevant id appears in the first k retrieved.

retrieved = [[3, 1, 7], [2, 9, 4], [5, 6, 0]]
relevant  = [{1},       {4},       {8}]
recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, 2)   # 1/3: only question 0 has a hit in its top 2

tests.name: example
tests.code:
out = recall_at_k([[3, 1, 7], [2, 9, 4], [5, 6, 0]], [{1}, {4}, {8}], 2)
assert abs(out - 1/3) < 1e-9, f'expected 1/3 (only the first question has a relevant id in its top 2), got {out}'

tests.name: larger k can only help
tests.code:
out = recall_at_k([[3, 1, 7], [2, 9, 4], [5, 6, 0]], [{1}, {4}, {8}], 3)
assert abs(out - 2/3) < 1e-9, f'with k=3 question 1 also hits (id 4 is third), so 2/3; got {out}'

tests.name: one hit is enough
tests.code:
out = recall_at_k([[1, 2]], [{1, 2}], 2)
assert out == 1.0, f'a question counts once even if several relevant ids are retrieved; expected 1.0, got {out}'

tests.name: k = 1
tests.code:
out = recall_at_k([[5, 1], [4, 2]], [{1}, {4}], 1)
assert out == 0.5, f'only the top result counts when k=1: question 1 hits, question 0 misses; got {out}'

hints: any(i in good for i in ranked[:k]) is True when there is at least one hit.

problems.title: Blend dense and keyword search
problems.prompt:
Reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack et al., 2009) merges several ranked lists without needing their scores to be comparable. Each list gives a document 1 / (c + rank), with rank starting at 1 and the constant c = 60; a document's fused score is the sum over the lists it appears in.

Write rrf(rankings, c=60) that returns all documents sorted by fused score, best first (break ties by document id, smallest first, so the answer is deterministic).

dense   = ['a', 'b', 'c']
keyword = ['c', 'a', 'd']
rrf([dense, keyword])   # ['a', 'c', 'b', 'd']

tests.name: example
tests.code:
out = rrf([['a', 'b', 'c'], ['c', 'a', 'd']])
assert out == ['a', 'c', 'b', 'd'], f"expected ['a', 'c', 'b', 'd'], got {out}. 'a' is 1st and 2nd, 'c' is 3rd and 1st: 1/61+1/62 > 1/63+1/61."

tests.name: single list keeps its order
tests.code:
out = rrf([['x', 'y', 'z']])
assert out == ['x', 'y', 'z'], f'one ranking fused with nothing should keep its order, got {out}'

tests.name: agreement wins
tests.code:
out = rrf([['p', 'q'], ['q', 'p'], ['q', 'r']])
assert out[0] == 'q', f'q is near the top of every list and should come first, got {out}'

tests.name: every document appears once
tests.code:
out = rrf([['a', 'b'], ['b', 'c'], ['d']])
assert sorted(out) == ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] and len(out) == 4, f'each document should appear exactly once, got {out}'

hints: sorted(scores, key=lambda d: (-scores[d], d)) sorts by score descending, then by id.
